Topic: databases

Where an application keeps its data, taught from zero: follow one product's data from a file on disk to a fleet of specialised stores, and learn what each kind of database is for, how it works inside, and what it costs. Sources are linked inline; data as of October 2026.
One screen1 Why a database2 SQL3 Transactions4 Inside5 Rows and columns6 Families7 Choosing8 ML and LLMsHow a pro choosesGlossary

One app's data, from a file to a fleet, in one screen

About 27 minutes to read (7,100 words; the glossary at the end can be skimmed), plus the optional animations. It starts from zero: every term is explained where it first appears and collected in the Glossary. Numbers marked measured were measured for this page on a laptop; numbers marked illustrative are made up to show a shape.

A database is a program whose whole job is to keep an application's data safe, correct and quick to find while many people use it at once. This page follows one product's data as it grows, and lets each problem arrive before the idea that fixes it.

The running example is the same one the Topic: swe-and-system-design page uses: a chat assistant powered by a large language model (LLM). People sign up (users), open conversations (chats), send and receive messages, and spend prepaid credits. The picture shows where that data lives at three moments in the product's life.

Each store is coloured by the section that introduces it. Do not worry about the names yet; each is explained in its section.

The eight sections, one line each

Why not just a fileA file loses writes, breaks on a crash and must be read whole. A database promises the opposite; the relational model organises data into tables linked by keys. SQL from zeroYou say what you want, not how to get it. Six clauses cover most queries; keep one fact in one place. TransactionsTwo requests at once can spend the same credit twice. A transaction makes a group of changes all-or-nothing and isolated; the isolation level says which mix-ups you still allow. Inside the engineData lives in 8 KB pages. A log written before the pages survives crashes; a B-tree index finds one row in a few page reads; the planner picks how to run your query. Rows and columnsApps fetch whole rows; analytics sums one column over millions of rows. Stored by column, the same answer here needed about 94 times fewer bytes. The familiesKey-value, document, wide-column, search, vector, time-series, graph, embedded, distributed SQL: each is an escape hatch from Postgres for one specific problem, with a price. ChoosingFive questions decide the store; two decisions (the shard key and the partition key) cannot be walked back. The ML and LLM angleVectors next to your rows for RAG, feature stores as two ordinary databases, DuckDB on Parquet, and a language model that writes query plans.
The one idea to keep
Start with one PostgreSQL database (Postgres for short: a free, open-source relational database) and add another kind of store only when a measured problem forces you to. Every extra store is a second copy of some fact, and copies drift apart. A professional can name, for each store in the fleet, the problem that justified it and what it costs.

Three tabs sit beside this one. SQL playground runs real SQL on the chat tables in your browser. Query plans shows how Postgres actually executed real queries on a 10-million-message table. Database atlas compares every family and the main products in detail.

1. Why not just a file

The problem appears

Day one, the chat app keeps everything in one file, chats.json: the server reads it when it starts, changes it in memory, and writes the whole file back after every message. It works for you alone. Then three things go wrong, each at a different number.

  • Two requests at once lose a write. You send a message from your phone and your laptop in the same second. Both requests read the file, each adds its own message, each writes the whole file back: the second write replaces the first, and one message is gone with no error.
  • A crash in the middle breaks the file. The power goes out half-way through writing; the file is now half old, half new, and may not even parse.
  • Every question reads everything. "Show user 17's chats" means loading and scanning the whole file. At a thousand messages nobody notices; at ten million messages (a few gigabytes) every page view reads gigabytes. illustrative

The idea: a database makes four promises

A database (properly a database management system) is a separate program that owns the data and lets many clients use it at once. Your app sends it requests over a connection instead of touching files. In exchange it promises four things a file cannot:

DurabilityOnce it says "saved", the data survives a crash or a power cut (section 4 shows how).
Safe concurrent accessMany requests at once cannot overwrite each other's work by accident (section 3).
QueriesYou ask a question ("user 17's chats, newest first") and it finds the answer without reading everything (sections 2 and 4).
ConstraintsRules the data must always obey ("every message belongs to an existing chat", "a balance is never negative"), checked on every write.

The relational model in plain words

Most databases you will meet first are relational: the data sits in tables, one per kind of thing. A table has named columns (the fields) and rows (one per thing). Each row has a primary key, a value that identifies it uniquely, usually a number called id. A row points to a row of another table by storing that row's key: a foreign key. That pointer is the "relation". The idea is from Edgar Codd's 1970 paper (Codd, CACM 1970); its lasting point is that you describe data as tables and ask for what you want, and the system decides how to fetch it.

The chat product needs four tables. Click any row: the rows it points to, and the rows that point to it, light up.

Click a row to follow its keys.

Notice what is not there: the message row does not repeat the user's email or name. It stores only chat_id; the chat stores user_id; the email lives once, in users. Section 2 explains why that matters.

What it costs
A separate server to run, back up and upgrade; a network hop on every request (a fraction of a millisecond in the same data centre); and a schema (the declared tables, columns and rules) that you change through deliberate migrations rather than by editing a file. For anything more than a prototype the trade is overwhelmingly worth it. When you want the promises without a server, an embedded database such as SQLite runs inside your program and stores everything in one file (section 6).
Go deeper (optional): type the tables above into the SQL playground; how to design tables, keys and relationships (modelling, normalisation, migrations) is on the child page SQL and data modelling; for the API that sits in front of the database, see Building a backend API.

2. SQL from zero

The problem appears

The data is in tables now; the app needs to ask questions of it. "The last 50 messages of chat 11." "How many tokens did each user's replies use this month?" You could write a loop for each question, but then every new question is new code, and the loop decides how to search, which is the part a database is good at.

The idea: say what you want, not how to get it

SQL (Structured Query Language) is the language relational databases speak. It is declarative: you describe the result you want, and the database works out the steps (section 4 shows how it chooses). Six pieces cover most of what an app does:

SELECT id, role, tokens          -- which columns
FROM messages                     -- which table
WHERE chat_id = 11                -- which rows
ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 50;       -- in what order, how many

JOIN combines rows of two tables whose keys match, which is how the foreign keys of section 1 get used. GROUP BY collapses rows that share a value into one row per value, with an aggregate such as count(*) or sum(tokens) computed over each group. Changing data uses three more statements:

INSERT INTO messages (chat_id, role, tokens) VALUES (11, 'user', 14);
UPDATE chats SET title = 'SQL basics' WHERE id = 11;
DELETE FROM messages WHERE chat_id = 13;

A query is written in one order and evaluated in another. The database starts from the tables (FROM and the joins), filters (WHERE), groups, computes the SELECT list, then sorts; the PostgreSQL SELECT reference lists this processing order. The animation runs one real query on the sample rows from section 1, one clause at a time.









The rows are the nine sample messages above; every intermediate table is computed live from them. Chen disappears at the WHERE step because his only message is from the user, not the assistant: a filter removes rows before any grouping happens.




Rules the data must obey: schema and constraints


The schema is the declared shape of the tables. Constraints in it are checked on every write, so bad data cannot get in, whichever code path tries:


CREATE TABLE messages (
  id      INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,                   -- unique, never empty
  chat_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES chats(id),  -- must name an existing chat
  role    TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (role IN ('user', 'assistant')),
  tokens  INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (tokens >= 0)
);


Inserting a message for chat 999, which does not exist, shows a constraint doing its job: Postgres refuses it. Try it in lesson 9 of the SQL playground, which runs SQLite: SQLite accepts the orphan row until foreign keys are switched on with PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON, a default worth knowing.


One fact in one place: normalisation


Suppose, to save a join, every message row also stored the user's email. Ada changes her email: now ten thousand message rows must change, and if one code path forgets, the database holds two emails for one person and nothing says which is right. That is an update anomaly. Normalisation is the discipline of storing each fact once (the email in users, a pointer everywhere else) so that a change is one write. Codd defined the normal forms that make this precise in 1970 and 1971; for daily work the one-line rule is enough.


What it costs
Reading normalised data means joins, which cost work at query time. Copying facts on purpose to avoid joins is denormalisation: it makes reads faster and makes you responsible for keeping every copy in step. Analytics stores (section 5) and wide-column stores (section 6) denormalise deliberately; an app's source of truth usually should not. SQL itself has dialects: the basics above work everywhere, but details (date functions, upserts, JSON operators) differ between Postgres, MySQL and SQLite.


Go deeper (optional): every query here runs in the SQL playground; the PostgreSQL tutorial chapters 2 and 3 (about 1 hour) teach the same statements on a weather example; joins, grouping, window functions and recursive queries in depth, with 28 graded exercises, are on the child page SQL and data modelling.







3. Transactions: when two requests touch the same data


The problem appears


Ben has 1 credit left. He has the chat open in two browser tabs and presses send in both within the same instant. The server code for "send a message" is reasonable on its own: read Ben's balance; if it is above zero, call the model, save the reply, and write the balance minus one. Two copies of that code run at the same time, both read 1, both decide Ben can pay, both write 0. Ben got two answers for one credit.


This is not a thought experiment. Run against a real Postgres for this page (two sessions, each wrapped in BEGIN and COMMIT, the second starting 0.1 seconds after the first; the script gave Ben's credits row user_id 17 instead of the sample table's 2, which changes nothing): both messages were saved and the balance ended at 0 measured. The same bug shows up as two people booking the last seat, or two withdrawals from one account. Its name is a lost update: one transaction's write silently overwrote a decision based on a value that was already stale.


The idea: transactions, and how isolated they are


A transaction is a group of reads and writes that the database treats as one unit: you say BEGIN, do the work, and say COMMIT (keep it all) or ROLLBACK (undo it all). The guarantees are summed up as ACID, a name from Haerder and Reuter's 1983 survey (ACM Computing Surveys):




AtomicAll of the transaction happens, or none of it. Saving the reply without charging the credit cannot happen.


ConsistentEvery constraint holds after each commit (a balance below zero is refused). Consistency of your business rules is still your code's job.


IsolatedTransactions running at the same time do not see each other's half-done work. How isolated is a setting, and it is the hard part.


DurableOnce committed, it survives a crash (section 4).




The measured run above was inside transactions, and Ben still paid once for two answers. That is because Postgres's default isolation level, read committed, lets each statement see everything committed before it started, including another transaction's commit made after yours began. Stronger levels forbid more mix-ups and cost more. The useful way to read them is by the anomaly (the mix-up) each one prevents, as the Postgres documentation tabulates:




Level in PostgresDirty read
see uncommitted data		Non-repeatable read
same row, two values		Phantom
new rows appear		Serialization anomaly
e.g. write skew


Read committed (default)nopossiblepossiblepossible


Repeatable readnonono in Postgres (the SQL standard allows it)possible


Serializablenononono




Read uncommitted exists in the SQL standard, but Postgres runs it as read committed. Write skew is the subtle one: two transactions each read a set of rows, each make a decision that is valid alone, and write different rows, so neither overwrites the other yet the combination breaks a rule (two doctors both going off call because each saw the other on call). It was named in Berenson et al., 1995.


The animation replays Ben's two tabs three ways: unprotected, with a row lock, and at the strictest level.


















How a database isolates without stopping everyone: MVCC


The naive way to isolate is to lock everything a transaction touches, so everyone else waits. Postgres, like most modern databases, instead keeps several versions of a row: an update writes a new version and leaves the old one for transactions that started earlier. Each statement (or, at repeatable read and above, each transaction) reads a consistent snapshot, so, in the documentation's words, "reading never blocks writing and writing never blocks reading" (Postgres MVCC). This is MVCC, multi-version concurrency control. Two writers to the same row still conflict: one waits for the other, or, at the stricter levels, one is told to retry.


The three fixes, in the order a professional reaches for them


    

  1. Make the check part of the write: UPDATE credits SET balance = balance - 1 WHERE user_id = 2 AND balance > 0 (Ben is user 2 in the sample tables), then call the model only if one row changed. Under read committed, a second update waits for the first and re-checks its condition on the new row (Postgres docs, read committed), so only one succeeds. One statement, no new concepts.
    2. 

  2. Lock what you are about to change: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks the row until commit; the second tab waits, then reads 0.
    3. 

  3. Ask for serializable and retry: the database detects any interleaving that could not have happened one transaction at a time and aborts one transaction with a serialization error; your code must retry it. This protects even against anomalies you did not think of, such as write skew.
    4. 



What it costs
Locks make other transactions wait, and two transactions waiting on each other's locks is a deadlock (the database kills one). Serializable turns conflicts into errors your code must retry. Old row versions pile up until a background clean-up (VACUUM in Postgres) removes them, and a transaction left open for hours stops that clean-up. Keep transactions short: never hold one open while waiting on a model call. And guarantees are only as good as the implementation: Jepsen found that Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL multi-AZ clusters violated snapshot isolation (Jepsen, 2025-04-29), where single-node Postgres did not. Defaults differ between products too: MySQL's default level is repeatable read, which Jepsen found weaker than its name (Jepsen, MySQL 8.0.34). Check the default of whatever you run.

4. Inside the engine: pages, the log, the index, the planner


The problem appears


The messages table reaches a million rows. Opening a chat runs "the messages of chat 42000", and on the laptop measured for this page that query read 19,349 pages and took 28 ms measured to return 6 rows. Every chat opened by every user pays that, and it grows with the table. Meanwhile section 1 promised that "saved" survives a power cut, yet writing to disk is slow. Both problems are solved inside the engine, and knowing the four pieces below is what lets you read a slow query instead of guessing.



Pages and the buffer pool


A database does not store rows one by one. Postgres keeps every table and index as an array of fixed-size pages, usually 8 KB each (Postgres page layout), and always reads and writes whole pages. The million-message table is 19,235 pages (157 MB) measured; each page holds about 52 rows. Pages in use are kept in RAM in the buffer pool (in Postgres, shared_buffers, 128 MB by default and commonly set to about a quarter of the machine's memory, Postgres docs). The reason it matters: reading memory takes about 100 nanoseconds, a random read from a fast SSD about 100 microseconds, a thousand times longer (see the Numbers to know tab of the system design page). Of the 19,349 page reads above, 14,435 were found in the buffer pool and 4,914 had to come from the operating system, because a 157 MB table does not fit in 128 MB.



The write-ahead log: how "saved" survives a crash


Writing every changed page to disk at every commit would be slow (random writes all over the disk) and still unsafe: a crash between two page writes leaves half a transaction on disk. The fix is the write-ahead log (WAL): before any data page changes on disk, a description of the change is appended to a sequential log file and forced to the disk with fsync (the operating-system call that waits until bytes are really on stable storage). The commit is acknowledged once the log record is safe; the changed pages are written later, in bulk, at a checkpoint. After a crash the database replays the log from the last checkpoint and redoes anything missing (Postgres WAL: "roll-forward recovery, also known as REDO").














One transaction from section 3: save Ben's reply (a page of messages) and charge his credit (a page of credits). The power fails at the same moment in both runs. The order of events is the mechanism Postgres documents; the drawing is illustrative.




The log is one of the most reused ideas in data systems: the same records, shipped to another machine, keep a replica (a full copy of the database on another machine) up to date; replayed to a chosen moment, they restore a backup to that moment; read by another program, they become a stream of changes. Waiting for the fsync is the cost of durability: on this page's laptop a small write transaction took 6.3 ms with a real flush against 0.42 ms without one measured (the Numbers to know tab has both and server SSDs, which flush far faster). Because one fsync can cover many transactions committing at once, a busy database pays it less than once per commit: with real flushes the same laptop ran 148 write transactions per second from one client and 2,133 from 32 clients measured (pgbench, run for the Database atlas).



The B-tree index: a few page reads instead of all of them


An index is a separate structure, kept sorted by some column, that maps each value to where its rows are, like the index at the back of a book. The default kind is the B-tree: a tree of pages, each holding hundreds of sorted keys, so even millions of rows sit only three or four levels below the root (Postgres B-tree). Finding a value means reading one page per level, then the table pages that hold the matching rows. The animation runs the same lookup without and with CREATE INDEX ON messages (chat_id).


















What an index costs
Every insert and update must also update every index on the table, so writes get slower with each index; indexes take space (9.3 MB here, 6% of the table measured); and an index only helps queries that filter or sort on its leading column. Index the columns your queries search by, measure, and drop indexes nobody uses.



The planner, and how to ask it what it did


Because SQL says what, not how, something must choose how. The query planner (or optimiser) considers alternative plans (scan the whole table or use an index; which table to join first; which join method) and estimates the cost of each from statistics it keeps about the data, such as row counts and common values. It runs the cheapest estimate. EXPLAIN shows the chosen plan, and EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs it and adds the real row counts and times (Using EXPLAIN). For the lookup above it prints Index Scan using messages_chat_idx on messages ... (actual rows=6) with Buffers: shared hit=12.


The planner goes wrong when its estimates do: statistics that are stale after a bulk load, or two columns that are correlated (city and country) when it assumes they are independent. The habit that finds the problem is to compare estimated rows with actual rows at each step of the plan; the lowest step where they diverge badly is where to look.


What the planner costs
Planning takes time on every query (a fraction of a millisecond for simple ones; prepared statements reuse plans), and a plan that was right yesterday can go wrong after the data changes. You trade control for convenience: most of the time that is a good trade.


Go deeper (optional): real plans for real queries on a 10-million-message table, with estimates against actual rows, are in Query plans; the families of storage engines (B-tree against LSM-tree) are compared in Database atlas; pages, the WAL, B-trees against LSM-trees and every index type are on the child page Storage engines and indexes; how the planner prices plans, why its estimates go wrong and how to fix a slow query are on Query planning and performance; backups, replicas and keeping a server healthy are on Running Postgres in production.







5. Rows and columns: apps and analytics want opposite layouts


The problem appears


The product team asks a new kind of question: "how many tokens did each model produce this month?" It touches every message but needs only two of its seven columns. On the million-message table, Postgres read 157.7 MB (19,251 pages) in 70 ms measured to answer it, because every page holds whole rows, including the message text the question never looks at. At a billion messages that is about 158 GB read per question (derived, scaling linearly), on the same server that is answering users.


The two kinds of work have names. OLTP (online transaction processing) is what the app does: many small reads and writes, each touching a few whole rows (open a chat, save a message), each expected in milliseconds. OLAP (online analytical processing) is what analytics does: few, large queries that read a few columns of a huge number of rows and aggregate them. A layout that is good for one is bad for the other.


The idea: store each column together


A row store such as Postgres keeps each row's values side by side, so fetching one whole row is one page read. A column store keeps all values of one column side by side, so a query reads only the columns it names. Values of one column look alike, so they also compress far better: the role column, which alternates between two words, shrank from 254,530 bytes to 862 measured. The animation answers the same question both ways, on the same million messages: once from Postgres's pages, once from a Parquet file (an open, column-oriented file format: each column of each block of rows is stored and compressed separately, with min and max values recorded so whole blocks can be skipped; Parquet docs) read by DuckDB (a column-oriented analytical database that runs inside your program, like a library, with no server; duckdb.org).


















Both runs return the same four totals (for example 80,277,256 tokens for mini). The column store read about 94 times fewer bytes. Bytes are the fair comparison here; the times come from two different engines and are shown only as a sanity check. Query plans repeats the measurement at 10 million messages: 1.47 GB read by Postgres against 17.3 MB of two Parquet columns, 87 times fewer bytes and about 50 times faster.


What it costs
Changing one row means rewriting compressed blocks, so column stores are built for appending in bulk, not for updating single rows; reading one whole message touches seven separate column chunks. And the analytics copy is a second copy: something must move the data from Postgres into it (a nightly export, or a stream of changes), and it is always somewhat behind. That is why the fleet picture puts the column store beside Postgres, never instead of it.


Where it runs: DuckDB on Parquet files is the laptop and single-machine end (it happily reads tens of gigabytes); ClickHouse is a column-store server you run yourself; BigQuery, Snowflake and Redshift are managed services that keep storage and compute separate; a lakehouse is Parquet files on cloud object storage plus a table format (Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake) that adds safe concurrent updates, so several engines can read the same files.


Go deeper (optional): the analytical stores side by side are in Database atlas; moving data out of Postgres reliably (change streams, the outbox pattern) is on Queues, streams and async work; column stores, Parquet, DuckDB, ClickHouse and lakehouse tables in depth are on the child page Analytics: columnar engines, DuckDB and the lakehouse.







6. The families: escape hatches from the Postgres default


The problem appears


The product keeps growing, and some requests stop fitting one relational database well: the chat list is rebuilt from the same expensive query thousands of times a minute; users want to search their history by words and by meaning; the operations team stores a latency measurement every second from every server. Each of these has a kind of database built for it. The names multiply quickly (there are hundreds of products), but there are only about nine families, and each exists because of one specific problem.


The idea: a family is a data model plus a storage layout tuned for one access pattern


Read each card as: which problem forces you here, what you pay, and what it would hold in the chat product. Postgres can do a passable version of several of them through extensions, which is why it stays the default until a measurement says otherwise.




Key-value: Redis, Valkey, DynamoDB
Get and set a value by its key, nothing else. Redis keeps everything in memory, so a lookup is a few microseconds of work plus the network hop; writing to disk is optional (Redis persistence). DynamoDB is Amazon's managed, replicated version that grows without limit if every access names its key.
Forced by: the same answer read over and over, counters and rate limits, sessions. Costs: no queries beyond the key; as a cache it is a second copy that goes stale (animation below); Redis copies to its replicas asynchronously by default, so a failover can lose writes it already acknowledged (Redis replication). Chat product: the cached chat list, per-user rate limits.


Document: MongoDB, Firestore
Each record is a nested JSON-like document, read and written whole, with no fixed schema.
Forced by: records whose shape varies a lot and is always read as one unit. Costs: joins and multi-document transactions are weaker or slower; "no schema" becomes many schemas over time. Postgres stores and indexes JSON too (jsonb, Postgres JSON types), which covers most cases. Chat product: tool-call payloads of varied shape, usually a jsonb column instead.


Wide-column: Cassandra, ScyllaDB, Bigtable
Rows grouped by a partition key that decides which machine holds them, sorted inside the partition; you design one table per query rather than normalising (Cassandra data modelling).
Forced by: write volume beyond one machine, many regions, queries known in advance. Costs: no joins, no new queries without a new table, and the partition key can only be changed by rewriting all the data. Chat product: messages at a scale few products reach.


Search: Elasticsearch, OpenSearch
An inverted index maps each word to the documents containing it, like a book index for every word; results are ranked with BM25, a scoring formula that rewards words frequent in the document and rare in the collection (the default in Elasticsearch, Elastic docs).
Forced by: "find messages mentioning invoice", typo tolerance, facets. Costs: another copy, updated with a delay of about a second, that must be rebuildable from the source of truth. Postgres full-text search is enough for modest volumes, but its built-in ranking (ts_rank) is not BM25: it has no rarity weight (Postgres docs). Chat product: search over chat history.


Vector: pgvector, Qdrant, Milvus, Pinecone
Stores embeddings (lists of numbers a model produces so that similar meanings get nearby lists) and finds the nearest ones to a query's embedding, approximately, to be fast. Section 8 covers when the Postgres extension is enough.
Forced by: search by meaning, retrieval for an LLM (RAG). Costs: results are approximate; indexes are large and slow to build. Combining word ranking and vectors (hybrid search) is not always a win: in Search and vector databases, scored by nDCG@10 (0 to 1, how good the top 10 results are), vectors alone beat the fusion on Quora questions (0.839 against 0.825) while the fusion won on SciFact (0.714 against 0.645 for vectors) measured. Chat product: "find past chats about this topic", documents for RAG.


Time-series: TimescaleDB, InfluxDB, Prometheus
Timestamped measurements appended in time order, stored in time-sliced chunks, compressed, summarised and deleted on a schedule.
Forced by: metrics at a steady high rate with "last hour" queries. Costs: poor at anything that is not a time range; a column store such as ClickHouse often does the same job. Chat product: latency and tokens-per-second for every request.


Graph: Neo4j, Memgraph
Nodes and edges stored so that following an edge is cheap, for questions about paths and patterns of unknown depth ("the shortest chain of friends from Ada to Chen").
Forced by: path and pattern queries of variable depth (fraud rings, permissions inherited through groups, knowledge graphs). Measured on a friends graph in NoSQL in practice, Neo4j found a 4-hop shortest path in 5 ms against about 130 ms for a recursive query in Postgres measured. Costs: another system; and it does not win at counting: for "friends of friends" (up to three hops) Postgres joins were the fastest of the engines tried. Chat product: rarely needed.


Embedded: SQLite, DuckDB
A library inside your program, storing data in a local file: no server, no network. SQLite (rows) is likely the most deployed database of all, with over a trillion databases in use (sqlite.org); DuckDB (columns) is its analytics counterpart.
Forced by: a phone or desktop app, tests, notebooks, a single-machine job. Costs: one machine; SQLite allows one writer at a time (When to use SQLite). Chat product: chat history cached on the phone; analysis in a notebook.


Distributed SQL: CockroachDB, Spanner, TiDB, YugabyteDB
SQL and transactions across many machines and regions; each slice of data is copied to several machines that agree on every change through a consensus protocol (Raft or Paxos).
Forced by: writes or data beyond one Postgres machine, or surviving the loss of a whole region, without giving up SQL. Costs: every write waits for machines to agree (more latency, especially across regions); transactions spanning slices are slower; more to pay and run. Chat product: only at very large scale.




The most common escape hatch by far is the first one, used as a cache: a fast store in front of the database holding copies of answers already computed. Each cached entry usually carries a TTL (time to live) after which it expires. The animation shows what a copy costs. Ada reads her chat list, renames a chat, and reads the list again.














The sequence of events is illustrative. A cache pays off only for answers that are expensive to compute: on the laptop measured for the system design page, a Postgres lookup by primary key took 0.067 ms over a local connection, while the Redis documentation's own benchmark example shows about 0.14 ms per request (vendor figure, different conditions); caching a single-row lookup by key buys nothing. Even "delete on write" has a race: a slow reader can put an old value back just after the delete, which is why production caches add an expiry as a backstop (Scaling Memcache at Facebook).




What every extra family costs
Each one is a second copy of some facts with its own lag, its own failure modes, backups, upgrades and on-call knowledge. The question is never "is this tool better at X" but "is X now painful enough, measured, to pay for another system".

7. Choosing: five questions, and two doors that only open one way


The problem appears


Every database vendor's benchmark shows its product winning. Comparisons by category ("we need a NoSQL database") lead to systems chosen for the wrong reason, and a database is one of the hardest things to change later: the data has to move, and every piece of code that talks to it has to change. So the choice needs a method, applied when a measured limit forces you off the default.


The idea: five questions, in this order




1. What are the access patterns?Which queries run, how often, and how fast they must be. Start here, not from the shape of the data: almost any data fits almost any model, but each store is fast only at certain queries. A key-value store is cheap only if you always know the key.


2. Which rules must hold across rows?If two things must change together or not at all (charge a credit and save a reply), you want real transactions, inside one store. This one question rules out most alternatives for most business data.


3. How much writing, and how uneven?Steady thousands of small writes per second fit one Postgres server: even this page's laptop, flushing every commit to its SSD for real, ran 2,133 small write transactions per second with 32 clients measured (Database atlas has the run), and a server SSD flushes far faster. Hundreds of thousands per second across regions do not fit. Plan for the peak and the busiest single key, not the average.


4. How much do you know about future questions?If you cannot list tomorrow's queries, a normalised relational schema lets you ask new ones for free. Only queries known and frozen justify a store designed around them.


5. What can your team run at 3 a.m.?Backups that have actually been restored, failover, upgrades, someone on call who understands it. A database nobody can debug under load is the wrong database, whatever its benchmarks. What this takes for Postgres is on Running Postgres in production.




Applied to the chat product, the answers explain the fleet in the opening picture:




DataAccess patternRules across rowsStore


Users, chats, messages, creditsBy user and chat; new questions every monthYes: credits and replies change togetherPostgres (the source of truth)


Chat list, rate-limit countersSame key read constantly; a little staleness is fineNoRedis, as a cache built from Postgres


Tokens per model per dayScans of two columns over everythingNo; minutes behind is fineColumn store, copied from Postgres


Search history by meaningNearest neighbours of an embeddingMust respect who may see which chatpgvector inside Postgres first (section 8)




The two doors that only open one way


Almost every choice above can be undone with a migration: expensive, but finite. Two cannot be undone without rewriting every row. When data is split across machines (sharding), the shard key decides which machine each row lives on: shard the chat product by user and "all of one user's chats" is fast while "all chats about a topic, across users" must ask every machine. In a wide-column store, the partition key plays the same role. Choose either from the queries you will run most, check that no single key will be too busy, and take time over it, because changing it later means moving all the data (Scaling a database chooses one for the chat product on real data, sections 7 and 9).


One more decision is cheapest at schema time: how long each kind of data is kept and how it is deleted. A user's right to have their data erased, rules about which country data may live in, and audit retention all become requirements on the store; a store with no practical way to delete one user's rows is one you will eventually have to migrate off.


What this method costs
It is slower than picking the newest tool, and it often ends with "stay on Postgres and add an index", which is less exciting to build. It also asks you to measure before deciding, which means building the measurement first.


Go deeper (optional): the families side by side, with the questions each answers well, are in Database atlas; choosing a shard key on the chat data, and why changing it is a one-way door, is on the child page Scaling a database; sharding and its trade-offs in general are on Distributed systems fundamentals; worked designs that make these choices end to end are on System design case studies.







8. The ML and LLM angle


The problem appears


The chat product adds retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): before answering, it finds the passages of a user's uploaded documents closest in meaning to the question and puts them in the prompt. Every passage now has an embedding, plus the facts any app needs: who owns it, who may see it, which document it came from, and a way to delete it when the document is deleted. Separately, the team trains models on chat logs and evaluates them, which means scanning large datasets.


Vectors next to the rows: pgvector first


Finding the exact nearest embeddings means comparing the question with every stored vector. Approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) indexes trade a little accuracy (recall: the share of the true nearest neighbours returned) for speed. The usual one is HNSW, a layered graph of vectors that a search walks greedily from a sparse top layer down to a dense bottom one (Malkov and Yashunin). pgvector adds a vector column type and HNSW and IVFFlat indexes to Postgres (version 0.8.7 as of 2026-10-04; pgvector README). That makes the passage, its owner, its permissions and its embedding one row: one transaction writes them together, one delete removes them, one backup holds them.


    

  • Limits worth knowing (from the README): the vector type can be indexed up to 2,000 dimensions, half-precision halfvec up to 4,000; HNSW defaults are m = 16, ef_construction = 64 and hnsw.ef_search = 40 (raise the last for better recall, slower queries).
    • 

  • Filtering is where it bites: with an approximate index, a WHERE condition (such as "only this user's documents") is applied after the index scan, so a selective filter can leave fewer results than asked for; version 0.8.0 added iterative scans that keep searching until enough rows pass.
    • 

  • Memory arithmetic: a 1,536-dimension embedding in 4-byte floats is 1,536 x 4 = 6,144 bytes (6,152 as pgvector stores it, with an 8-byte header), so a million passages need about 6.2 GB and a hundred million about 615 GB before any index (derived). Half precision halves it.
    • 



A dedicated vector database (Qdrant, Milvus, Pinecone and others) earns its place when the vectors outgrow what one Postgres server can hold and search fast, when filtered search dominates and needs filtering inside the graph walk, or when the index must scale separately from the rest of the data. The old version of this page put the line at roughly 10 million and 100 million vectors; those are rules of thumb nobody published a measurement for, so measure recall and latency on your own data instead.


Feature stores are two databases


A model in production needs the same input features it was trained on. A feature store (Feast, Tecton) is a naming convention over two ordinary stores: an offline store holding the history of feature values, used to build training sets and to load the online store, and an online store that serves features "at low latency" and keeps, "for each entity key, only the latest feature values" (Feast offline store, online store). In this page's terms: a column store (section 5) plus a key-value store (section 6), fed by the same code so training and serving do not drift apart.


DuckDB on Parquet for datasets and evals


Training data, eval results and logs are mostly Parquet files. DuckDB queries them in place, on a laptop or inside a job, with SQL and no server: the section 5 measurement read two columns of a million rows in 2.6 ms. On 2026-08-26 DuckLabs, the company that develops DuckDB, announced it would join AWS as a subsidiary, with DuckDB and its extensions staying MIT-licensed under the non-profit DuckDB Foundation (DuckDB announcement); the Database atlas records the deal closing on 2026-08-31.


A language model that writes query plans


Section 4's planner relies on estimates that are often wrong for joins. In September 2026 Rohan Bansal fine-tuned a 4-billion-parameter model (a Qwen 3.8 4B distillation) to write planner hints (for the pg_hint_plan extension) that steer Postgres's join order and join methods, trained on 13,646 queries of the Cardinality Estimation Benchmark and measured on the 113 queries of the Join Order Benchmark (write-up, 2026-09-16). Untrained, the model produced no usable plan for 99 of the 113 queries. Trained, taking the model's own pick per query gave a 1.40 times geometric-mean speedup over Postgres's planner, with 7 of 339 runs (113 queries x 3 runs) slower than Postgres; keeping the fastest candidate within one run (each candidate executed and timed) gave 1.44 times. The headline 1.81 times and 44.7% latency reduction, with none slower, come only from keeping the best of three separate runs (up to 15 candidates per query). Read every one of these with care: the Join Order Benchmark was also the set watched during development, so none of them is a held-out result. The whole project cost about $1,200 in GPU rental and API fees.


Two lessons transfer. The economics: executing several candidate plans costs far more than planning once, so this pays only for the same heavy analytic query run again and again, never for an app's small queries. And the method: the write-up warmed the cache until page hit and read counts were stable within 2% before timing anything, because query timings are easy to fake by accident with a warm or cold cache.


What it costs
Vectors are big (6 KB each at 1,536 dimensions) and their indexes are slow to build and hungry for memory; ANN results are approximate by design. A feature store is two systems kept in step. A learned planner adds a model, GPUs and a measurement harness to answer a question the built-in planner answers for free most of the time.


Go deeper (optional): retrieval quality, chunking and rerankers are on Topic: rag-and-retrieval; datasets and Parquet at training scale on Topic: data-curation-and-datasets; the planner model's training recipe on Topic: llm-training-and-post-training; serving and data paths for ML on ML system design; vector stores side by side in Database atlas; pgvector, ANN indexes and hybrid search, measured, are on the child page Search and vector databases; feature history, point-in-time joins and DuckDB in depth are on Analytics: columnar engines, DuckDB and the lakehouse.







How a pro chooses, in one list




1. Start with one Postgres and a normalised schema with keys and constraints, so the database refuses bad data whichever code path sends it (sections 1 and 2).


2. Put every check-then-change inside one statement or one short transaction: a conditional UPDATE ... WHERE balance > 0 first, a row lock or serializable-with-retry when the rule spans rows; never hold a transaction open across a model call (section 3).


3. Index for the queries you actually run, and read the plan: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), estimated against actual rows, pages read (section 4).


4. Move analytics off the app database into a column store fed from it, and accept that it lags (section 5).


5. Add a family only for a measured problem, and write down what it costs: the copy, its lag, its staleness and who runs it (section 6).


6. Treat the shard key and the partition key as permanent; everything else can be migrated (section 7).


7. Keep embeddings next to the rows they describe until a measurement says otherwise (section 8).


8. Trust, but test: restore a backup on a schedule (how, for Postgres: Running Postgres in production), and read what independent testers such as Jepsen found about the systems you run.








Glossary


Every term this page introduces, in the order it appears; each links to where it is explained.




Database: a program that owns data and lets many clients store and query it safely.


Relational: data as tables linked by keys, queried with SQL.


Table, row, column: one table per kind of thing, one row per thing, one column per field.


Primary key: the value that identifies a row uniquely.


Foreign key: a column holding another row's primary key; the link between tables.


Migration: a deliberate, versioned change to the schema.


SQL: the language of relational databases.


Declarative: describing the result, not the steps.


JOIN: combining rows of two tables whose keys match.


GROUP BY: one result row per distinct value, with aggregates such as count and sum.


Schema: the declared tables, columns and rules.


Constraint: a rule checked on every write (NOT NULL, CHECK, REFERENCES, UNIQUE).


Update anomaly: copies of one fact that disagree after a change.


Normalisation: storing each fact once.


Denormalisation: copying facts on purpose to make reads faster.


Lost update: a write based on a stale read silently overwriting another.


Transaction: reads and writes treated as one all-or-nothing unit.


ACID: atomic, consistent, isolated, durable.


Isolation level: how much concurrent transactions may see of each other; read committed, repeatable read, serializable.


Write skew: two transactions each valid alone, breaking a rule together.


MVCC: keeping several versions of a row so readers and writers do not block each other.


Deadlock: two transactions waiting on each other's locks; the database aborts one.


Page: the fixed-size block (8 KB in Postgres) data is stored and read in.


Buffer pool: the database's cache of pages in RAM.


Write-ahead log (WAL): changes appended to a log and flushed before data pages change; replayed after a crash.


fsync: the call that waits until written bytes are on stable storage.


Checkpoint: writing changed pages to the data files so the log can be trimmed.


Replica: a full copy of the database on another machine, kept current from the log.


Index: a sorted structure mapping values to the rows that hold them.


B-tree: the default index: a shallow tree of pages of sorted keys.


Query planner: the part that chooses how to run a query from cost estimates.


EXPLAIN: shows the chosen plan; with ANALYZE, the real counts and times.


OLTP: many small reads and writes of whole rows; what apps do.


OLAP: few large scans and aggregates over a few columns; what analytics does.


Row store / column store: rows kept together, or each column kept together.


Parquet: an open, compressed, column-oriented file format.


DuckDB: an in-process, column-oriented analytical database.


Lakehouse: Parquet files on object storage plus a table format that several engines share.


Partition key: the column that decides which machine holds a row in a wide-column store.


Inverted index: word to the documents that contain it.


BM25: the standard formula for ranking documents by the words they share with a query.


Embedding: a list of numbers a model produces so that similar meanings land close together.


Cache: a fast store holding copies of answers already computed.


TTL: time to live; when a cached entry expires.


Sharding: splitting data across machines by a shard key.


RAG: retrieving relevant passages and putting them in the model's prompt.


ANN: approximate nearest-neighbour search: fast, slightly inexact.


Recall: the share of the true nearest neighbours an ANN search returns.


HNSW: a layered graph index for ANN search.


pgvector: the Postgres extension for vector columns and ANN indexes.


Feature store: an offline history store plus an online latest-value store for model features.











SQL playground: learn SQL by running it


This tab holds a real database engine: SQLite (which its authors describe as the most widely deployed database engine), compiled to WebAssembly and running inside this page with no network. It is loaded with the chat product's data (50 users, 200 chats, 2,000 messages, one credits balance per user). Twelve short lessons take you from your first SELECT to transactions, each with a goal, a hint, a query you can edit and run, and what the result means.


Every lesson was also run, offline, on real PostgreSQL, the database the Reading tab recommends as the default. Its recorded result sits next to the live one, and where the two engines disagree the difference is the lesson: eight of the 45 menu choices differ, and each one is a trap that has bitten real teams.


Starting the in-page database...





The data: four tables


A table is a named set of rows with fixed columns. A primary key (PK) is a column whose value is unique and never empty, so it names exactly one row. A foreign key (FK) is a column holding another table's primary key: chats.user_id says which user owns the chat. That pointer is the "relation" in "relational database".




The exact schema (CREATE TABLE statements)
The same text creates the tables in both engines, except that Postgres declares each id as INTEGER GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY so it, like SQLite, picks the next id when an INSERT leaves it out. The rows come from a seeded generator (src/sql/gen_data.py): the same 2,300 rows every time, with a few gaps on purpose (5 users without a country, 6 users without chats, 37 chats without a title, 8 chats without messages) because gaps are where queries go wrong.


























Watch a JOIN match rows


The same four users and their chats, joined step by step. For each user on the left, the database looks for chats whose user_id equals that user's id, and writes one output row per match. Switch to LEFT JOIN to see the one difference: a user with no match still gets a row, with NULL in the chat columns.










Real rows from the lesson's data. A real engine does not always loop like this: with an index on chats.user_id it jumps straight to the matching chats, and on big tables it may build a hash table of one side first. The Query plans tab shows which method Postgres picks and why.

















Free play


Your own database: changes here persist between runs until you press Reset data. Write several statements separated by ;. Try a starter, or anything you like.





Ctrl or Cmd + Enter runs too.







How this tab was built and checked











Query plans: what the database actually does


You write SQL that says what you want; a part of the database called the planner decides how to get it: which table to read first, whether to use an index, how to match rows from two tables. The recipe it picks is the query plan. Here are eight real plans, measured on this page's chat product with 10 million messages, each before and after the change that fixes it.


How to read the numbers




Page
PostgreSQL stores every table and index in fixed blocks of 8 KB called pages. It never reads one row; it reads the page holding it. Counting pages is the honest way to measure work, because time depends on the machine and pages do not.


Buffer pool: "hit" and "read"
PostgreSQL keeps recently used pages in its own memory, the buffer pool (setting shared_buffers, 128 MB here). A page found there is a hit. A page it must ask the operating system for is a read; the operating system may still have it in its own memory, or may have to fetch it from the disk (case 8 shows the three).


Node
A plan is a tree of steps. Each box below is a node: the leaves read tables or indexes, the nodes above them combine, filter, sort or count what the leaves produce. Read a plan from the bottom up.


Estimated rows and actual rows
Before running, the planner guesses how many rows each node will produce, from statistics it keeps about every column. EXPLAIN ANALYZE then runs the query and reports what really happened. When the guess is far off, the planner may have chosen the wrong recipe (case 5).


Loops
How many times a node ran. A node on the inside of a nested loop runs once for every row from the outside, and its rows and time are per run.






















Pages being read, as the query runs 


hit: found in the buffer poolread: asked the operating system

    Child pages of this topic, in a beginner reading order
    

    Each one takes a section of this page to depth on the same chat product, with its own measurements. In this order, each assumes only this page and the ones before it.
    

    

    1. SQL and data modelling: queries, joins, schema design, normalisation, migrations
    Sections 1 and 2 in depth: how a query is evaluated, every kind of join, grouping, window functions, recursive queries, upserts, then modelling, normalisation, constraints, migrations that do not lock a live table, N+1 queries and SQL injection; 28 graded exercises. About 45 minutes.
    

    2. Transactions and concurrency: ACID, MVCC, isolation anomalies, locks
    Section 3 in depth: the eight anomalies, what each isolation level lets through (measured), MVCC, locks and deadlocks, optimistic concurrency, retries, long transactions. About 40 minutes.
    

    3. Storage engines and indexes: pages, B-trees, LSM-trees, the WAL, index types
    Section 4's engine in depth: pages, the buffer pool, the write-ahead log and a real crash recovery, B-trees against LSM-trees, every Postgres index type and shape, and what indexes cost on writes. About 43 minutes.
    

    4. Query planning and performance: EXPLAIN, statistics, slow queries, tuning
    Section 4's planner in depth: how a plan is priced, statistics and why estimates go wrong, join order, reading EXPLAIN, the slow-query workflow, the settings that matter, plan regressions, learned optimizers. About 45 minutes.
    

    5. Running Postgres in production: backups, replication, vacuum, upgrades, pooling
    Keeping the default database alive: backups and restores, replication and failover, vacuum and wraparound, connection pooling, upgrades, security and monitoring, with an incident lab. About 45 minutes.
    

    6. Scaling a database: read replicas, sharding Postgres, distributed SQL
    Section 7's one-way door in depth: the ladder from query fixes to read replicas, partitioning, sharding (choosing the shard key on real data) and distributed SQL, with how real companies climbed it. About 43 minutes.
    

    7. Caching: every layer, eviction, invalidation, and the LLM caches
    Section 6's cache card in depth: why caches work, every layer, invalidation and consistency windows, Redis eviction measured on real traffic, then the KV cache, provider prompt caching and semantic caching. About 45 minutes.
    

    8. Analytics: columnar engines, DuckDB and the lakehouse
    Section 5 in depth: column stores inside, the Parquet file byte by byte, DuckDB, ClickHouse, cloud warehouses, Iceberg and the lakehouse, ELT and dbt, and point-in-time joins for ML training data. About 42 minutes.
    

    9. NoSQL in practice: key-value, document, wide-column, time-series, graph
    Section 6's families in depth: Redis, DynamoDB single-table design, MongoDB beside Postgres jsonb, Cassandra, time series, graph databases measured against Postgres, embedded engines. About 45 minutes.
    

    10. Search and vector databases: inverted indexes, BM25, ANN, pgvector
    Section 6's search and vector cards and section 8's pgvector in depth: the inverted index, BM25, embeddings, ANN indexes measured for recall and latency, filtered and hybrid search, pgvector or a dedicated store. About 41 minutes.
    

    


    A reading path, from beginner to professional
    

    In order. Each step says when it pays to read it.
    

    

    1. PostgreSQL tutorial
    The official tutorial, PostgreSQL 18 (the current release; 19 is in beta): getting started, the SQL language, then views, foreign keys, transactions and window functions. Read first, with a local Postgres open. About 2 hours.
    

    2. Use The Index, Luke
    Markus Winand's free web book on indexing across Postgres, MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server and Db2: how an index works, the WHERE clause, joins, sorting, why a query does a full scan. After section 4, before your first slow-query hunt. About 4 hours.
    

    3. Using EXPLAIN
    PostgreSQL 18 manual, section 14.1: reading plans, costs, EXPLAIN ANALYZE, and how the planner's estimates are computed. The day a query is slow, alongside the Query plans tab. About 45 minutes.
    

    4. Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition
    Martin Kleppmann and Chris Riccomini, O'Reilly, March 2026 (author's site). The standard book on how data systems work and fail: data models, storage engines, replication, sharding, transactions, streams. After this page, a chapter at a time. About 15 hours.
    

    5. CMU 15-445/645 Database Systems
    Carnegie Mellon's introductory course, Fall 2026 taught by Jignesh Patel (25 lectures from the relational model to recovery and distributed databases; this semester's videos are on CMU's Panopto). Andy Pavlo's recorded Fall 2025 lectures are public on YouTube. When you want to know how an engine is built; the projects build one. About 30 hours of lectures.
    

    6. Database Internals
    Alex Petrov, O'Reilly, 2019. Part I is storage engines (B-trees, files, the log, LSM-trees); Part II distributed systems (failure detection, consensus). After DDIA, for the level below it. About 9 hours 30 minutes.
    

    7. Jepsen analyses
    Kyle Kingsbury's tests of what databases actually do under network faults and crashes, against what their documentation claims, with a map of consistency models. Recent: Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL 17.4 (2025). Before you choose or operate a system: read its analysis. About 1 hour per analysis.
    

    8. The Log: what every software engineer should know about real-time data's unifying abstraction
    Jay Kreps, LinkedIn Engineering, December 2013. Why one append-only log sits under replication, change streams and stream processing: section 4's WAL, generalised. The original LinkedIn address returned "not found" on 2026-10-04, so this is the Internet Archive's copy from June 2026. After section 4 and DDIA's chapter on streams. About 1 hour.
